item.title: UK-EU Summit: Britain's Big EU Summit Could've Been an Email
item.description: The most notable thing about Friday’s UK-EU summit, where British Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet the leaders of the European Union in Brussels, is that it needs to happen at all. The agreements likely to be announced — on food and agricultural trade and carbon-trading schemes — are hardly of earth-shattering consequence to the EU’s technocrats. For them, this meeting could have been an email.
item.dc:creator: Mihir Sharma

item.title: Italian Ski Slopes Really Do Not Need a KFC at The Top
item.description: Italy’s Dolomites are in the midst of a tourism boom, and there is nothing wrong with that. Still, opening a Kentucky Fried Chicken at the top of a ski slope in Cortina d’Ampezzo — co-host of the 2026 Winter Olympics — is an insult to mountain lovers like me. And my 12-year-old son agrees, so this isn’t just a middle-aged lament about unwanted change.
item.dc:creator: Tommaso Ebhardt

item.title: Nvidia's Fallout Is a Gift to Indian Billionaires Ambani and Adani
item.description: Silicon Valley’s nightmare week is turning into a windfall for India’s largest conglomerates. With Jensen Huang ousted from Nvidia Corp. following a scandal involving the chipmaker’s Singaporean cloud partner, Washington is slamming the door on Southeast Asian data centers suspected of funneling computing power to China. The crackdown could hand Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani an unexpected prize.
item.dc:creator: Andy Mukherjee

item.title: Proxy Wars Are the US-China-Russia Future
item.description: There were smiles and handshakes when US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met in China on Thursday for a rare three-way discussion of global security issues. “We are really making history,” the US president declared. This great-power summitry has triggered middle-power anxiety: US allies and partners worry, some quietly and some loudly, about the prospect of dirty deals that might carve up the globe.
item.dc:creator: Hal Brands

item.title: Chipdollars Are Reshaping US Dominance
item.description: The dollar may be on the cusp of a new era of hegemony that should silence the skeptics. But with its renewed resilience also comes increased volatility. That leaves economies increasingly vulnerable to lurches in US policy and the rapid evolution of the technology industry.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Moss

item.title: Three-Way Summit: Trump, Putin and Xi’s New World Order Has Arrived
item.description: There is a sense of inevitability to the images emerging from Shenzhen, where leaders of the world’s three largest military powers gathered around a table on Thursday, with China’s Xi Jinping at the center. This summit was bound to happen and, for all its lack of substance, marks something momentous: the passing of the old, liberal world order and Europe’s final humiliation.
item.dc:creator: Marc Champion

item.title: The NFL’s CTE Research Must Extend to Former High School Players
item.description: Most Americans who play tackle football never get anywhere near the National Football League. The vast majority don’t play past high school.

item.title: COP31: Do We Really Need 92,000 People at a Climate Conference?
item.description: A grand total of 55 delegates attended the US Constitutional Convention in 1787. An even smaller number of rebels met with England’s King John to bang out the Magna Carta in 1215. The point is that sometimes a relative handful of people can resolve big, knotty conflicts with novel, world-changing solutions.
item.dc:creator: Mark Gongloff

item.title: GM’s Next CEO Will Be Tested by Autonomy, Electrification
item.description: Succession planning is having a moment in Silicon Valley, and General Motors Co., ever eager to tout its technology chops, seems to be getting in on the act. The automaker has reportedly hired headhunters to find a replacement for Chief Executive Officer Mary Barra, who has run GM for almost 13 years. item.title: Anthropic Has Many More Shares to Come After Its IPO - Maybe Too Many
item.description: Bulging appetite for Anthropic PBC stock gave the Claude developer and its bankers confidence to price its colossal share offering above its stated price range. But it’s worth remembering the company needs strong sustained demand. There’s a huge amount of extra supply coming down the track as lockups expire on existing equity owners cashing in their riches.
item.dc:creator: Chris Hughes

item.title: Nvidia Scandals Make the Case for US Chip Controls
item.description: Congress is rightly demanding answers to many questions about the affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset that brought down Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang last week: Why didn’t the Federal Bureau of Investigation or the White House warn him about US concerns? What secrets might he have spilled? And what damage has the imbroglio done to national security?
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: FAA Network Outage Was a Normal Accident
item.description: The installation of a new router grounded America for four hours last week, even though 68 others just like it had previously been added to the Federal Aviation Administration’s network without incident. There’s a term for what happened last Friday: They’re called normal accidents — and the best way to protect against them is for managers to respect and empower the people who know the system best.
item.dc:creator: Gautam Mukunda

item.description: After staging a spectacular political comeback, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva must now quaff from a poisoned chalice holding the toxic fiscal cocktail he mixmastered during his third term.
